extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and students of history/sociology/political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic essay describing the social, military, legal, and demographic factors that make some nations prevail and others become 'arrested civilisations.' Identifies advantages (and dangers) that foster or impede long-term progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military strength growth
rubrics_metrics.description: The military strength of man has been growing from the earliest time known to our history, straight on till now.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military capability increases through constant acquisition of arms/techniques, imitation, competition and the coalescence of strengths; superiority in military art often determines which nations prevail. Examples: Roman legionaries vs earlier peoples, comparison across prehistoric evidence; guidance emphasizes long-term, cumulative improvements rather than isolated leaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantage-by-conquest mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: The strongest nation has always been conquering the weaker; every intellectual gain of a nation was used and 'invested' in war, so all else perished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conquest transmits or imposes military and cultural advantages; imitation of superior weapons and organisation spreads advantages. Use this mechanism to explain how specific advantages become decisive in intersocietal competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal fibre (existence of polity/law)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first thing to acquire is, if I may so express it, the LEGAL FIBRE; a polity first -- what sort of polity is immaterial; a law first -- what kind of law is secondary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A basic polity or law (a coercive habit or structure) binds people together and is the crucial early pre-requisite for civilisation. Even minimal legal structure that secures obedience/coherence can be decisive in early competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social coherence / tameness (self-domestication)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most obedient, the tamest tribes ... are, at the first stage in the real struggle of life, the strongest and the conquerors. The slightest symptom of legal development, the least indication of a military bond, is then enough to turn the scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection processes (akin to domestication) favor tribes that are more cohesive and obedient; social cohesion yields military advantage. Evaluate groups by their internal coherence and capacity to act collectively under law or command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of legality and variability
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning of civilisation is marked by an intense legality ... but that legality -- if it goes on -- kills out the variability implanted by nature. Progress is only possible where the force of legality has gone far enough to bind the nation together, but not far enough to kill out all varieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful societies preserve the stabilizing benefits of law while allowing variation/innovation; too much fixation (custom/religion) arrests development. Assess whether institutions permit controlled change without dissolving order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious/customary sanctions as arresting force
rubrics_metrics.description: Terrible religions ... put upon a fixed law a sanction so fearful that no one could dream of not conforming to it. No one will ever comprehend the arrested civilisations unless he sees the strict dilemma of early society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When religion or custom imposes inflexible sanctions that suppress variation, societies become 'arrested.' Use examples (Aztec religion, preserved archaic religions) to show how sacred sanctions maintain static social forms and block innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for semi-free discussion / standing system of debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Some 'standing system' of semi-free discussion is as necessary to break the thick crust of custom and begin progress as it is in later ages to carry on progress when begun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions permitting discussion and contest of ideas (even limited) help break ossified customs; evaluate presence/strength of forums, assemblies or other debate mechanisms that foster change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political constitution mix (monarchy/aristocracy/democracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the very earliest glimpses of Teutonic political life we find the monarchic, the aristocratic, and the democratic elements already clearly marked ... Such a system ... cherishes the principle of change while preserving sedateness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mixed constitution combining leadership, aristocratic stability, and popular participation encourages both discipline and adaptability; assess whether governance structures balance despotism's order and participatory elements' innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Despotism's early usefulness and later harm
rubrics_metrics.description: So long as war is the main business of nations, temporary despotism ... is indispensable. But despotism is unfavourable to the principle of variability; it tends to keep men in the customary stage of civilisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize despotism can be advantageous in early, warlike contexts (centralized command), yet it suppresses long-term variability and thus later progress; weigh short-term military gains against long-term stasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptiveness in law (legal adaptability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in her law itself no one can fail to see that, binding as was the habit of obedience, a hidden impulse of extrication DID manage ... to change the substance while conforming to the accidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The capacity to modify legal substance incrementally while retaining outward continuity helps societies evolve without breaking cohesion; evaluate how legal forms permit gradual adaptation (Rome as example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture of races (racial admixture) as source of variability
rubrics_metrics.description: The mixture of races sometimes brings out a form of character better suited than either parent form to the place and time ... it depends on the influences exercised by the MILIEU.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Racial or demographic mixing can produce increased variability and vigor, but outcomes depend on local conditions; use empirical observations (South America, France) to judge when admixture is advantageous versus harmful to social cohesion or morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of mixed moralities (cultural incompatibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: The union of the Englishman and the Hindoo produces something not only between races, but BETWEEN MORALITIES. They have no inherited creed or plain place in the world ... many mixtures must have wrought many ruins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether demographic/cultural mixing produces incompatible value-systems that undermine discipline and order; distinguish biologically advantageous admixture from socially disruptive moral divergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional institutions (e.g., slavery) as early advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Slavery ... is one of the institutions which, at a certain stage of growth, all nations in all countries choose and cleave to. Slaves only can give men leisure. Leisure is the great need of early societies, and slaves only can give men leisure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that some institutions (slavery) create short-term advantages (leisure, refinement, policy planning) that can aid early progress, particularly military/artistic originality, but impose severe long-term costs and moral evils; evaluate temporality and eventual harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leisure and class structure enabling refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: Refinement of feeling and repose of appearance have indeed no market value in the early bidding of nations ... but originality in war does, and slave-owning nations, having time to think, are likely to be more shrewd in policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions that free a class from manual labor (creating leisure) permit reflection, strategy and cultural production, which may confer advantages; weigh the benefits of leisure-enabled innovation against social injustice and eventual decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geography and exposure to competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary civilisation begins near the Mediterranean Sea ... geography long defied it. In such remote places there was no real competition, and on them inferior, half-combined men continued to exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regions exposed to rival polities (geographic proximity enabling competition) are likelier to experience selective pressures that drive progress; isolated regions may retain arrested civilisations due to lack of effective competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection/‘domestication’ processes in peoples
rubrics_metrics.description: The taming of animals ... is a kind of selection. Man, being the strongest of all animals, differs from the rest; he was obliged to be his own domesticator; he had to tame himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural and social selection over generations tends to favor less 'wild' traits (obedience/cohesion), producing societies better able to organise and prevail; use the domestication analogy to understand social evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion of social gains into military advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: One most important pre-requisite of a prevailing nation is that it should have passed out of the first stage of civilisation into the second stage ... and you cannot comprehend why progress is so slow till you see how hard the most obstinate tendencies of human nature make that step to mankind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether social, legal or cultural advantages (e.g., prophets, legal order) are actually invested in military/political power; Judaea is given as an example where combined variability and legality did not translate into military supremacy but produced lasting intellectual legacy.
